title: Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of multi-tenant saas architecture and its relationship to AWS Architecture and the Well-Architected Framework.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to multi-tenant saas architecture.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn multi-tenant saas architecture in the context of AWS Architecture and the Well-Architected Framework. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture matters because it is one part of aws architecture and well-architected reviews. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: AWS Well-Architected six pillars
content_blocks.alt_text: A balanced architecture review considers operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability.
content_blocks.caption: Use the six pillars to identify trade-offs and prioritize evidence-based improvements.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture belongs to AWS Architecture and the Well-Architected Framework. Architecture is a set of documented trade-offs across requirements, interfaces, security, scalability, reliability, operations and cost; review the evidence against the six Well-Architected pillars.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Tenant isolation; Shared and isolated resource models; Tenant identity and authorization; Metering and tenant-level cost analysis. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For multi-tenant saas architecture, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Tenant isolation
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: Shared and isolated resource models
items.text: Define the input/data permissions, expected evidence, evaluation cases, safety boundaries and cost limits. A generated answer or completed invocation is not by itself proof of correctness.

items.title: Tenant identity and authorization
items.text: State the principal, action, resource and applicable conditions. Prefer scoped permissions and temporary credentials, protect secrets, and collect evidence that access is both limited and usable.

items.title: Metering and tenant-level cost analysis
items.text: Estimate the complete workload, including requests, storage, data transfer and dependent services. Compare the estimate with actual usage and alerts; an alert is not a hard spend cap.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.
